q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>?
h: Draw the 5-carbon chain, then shorten it by one carbon and by two carbons, placing branches without duplicating.
w: Pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-methylbutane CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 and 2,2-dimethylpropane C(CH3)4: 3. A methyl on carbon 3 of butane or on the end carbon just redraws one of these.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>?
h: Longest chain 6, then 5 with one methyl, then 4 with two methyls. Rename each to catch duplicates.
w: Hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane: 5. Drawings such as 1-methylpentane or 2-ethylbutane are really hexane and 3-methylpentane, which is how students reach 6 or more.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O (count both alcohols and ethers)?
h: Place the –OH on each different carbon of the two C<sub>4</sub> skeletons, then place an O between carbons to make ethers.
w: Alcohols: 1-butanol, 2-butanol, 2-methyl-1-propanol (isobutyl alcohol), 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol) = 4. Ethers: diethyl ether, methyl propyl ether, isopropyl methyl ether = 3. Total 7. Choosing 4 counts only the alcohols.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>?
h: Keep the 3-carbon chain. Put both Cl on the same carbon, then on different carbons; check for repeats by numbering from the other end.
w: 1,1-dichloropropane, 2,2-dichloropropane, 1,2-dichloropropane and 1,3-dichloropropane: 4. 3,3- and 2,3- are just 1,1- and 1,2- numbered from the other end.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl?
h: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has two skeletons (butane and isobutane). How many different carbons can the Cl replace an H on in each?
w: Butane skeleton: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane. Isobutane skeleton: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (isobutyl chloride) and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl chloride). Total 4. Choosing 2 forgets the branched skeleton.

q: Counting cis and trans forms as separate compounds, how many open-chain alkenes have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>?
h: Find the different positions for C=C on butane and isobutane skeletons, then ask which one has two different groups on each double-bond carbon.
w: 1-Butene CH2=CHCH2CH3, 2-methylpropene CH2=C(CH3)2, and 2-butene CH3CH=CHCH3, which exists as cis and trans. 3 + 1 = 4. Choosing 3 ignores cis–trans; adding the rings cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane is wrong because they are not alkenes.

q: Not counting cis–trans isomers, how many open-chain alkenes have the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>?
h: Place the double bond in every distinct position on pentane, then on 2-methylbutane. 2,2-dimethylpropane has no room for C=C.
w: Pentane skeleton: 1-pentene, 2-pentene. 2-Methylbutane skeleton: 2-methyl-1-butene, 3-methyl-1-butene, 2-methyl-2-butene. Total 5. Answering 2 counts only the straight-chain skeleton and forgets the branched alkenes; 4 misses one of the branched ones.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O?
h: With one O and saturated carbons, the O can be in an –OH group or between two carbons (an ether).
w: 1-Propanol CH3CH2CH2OH, 2-propanol CH3CH(OH)CH3 and ethyl methyl ether CH3OCH2CH3: 3. Choosing 2 misses the ether.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count C and H in each. If the formulas match, are the atoms connected in the same order?
w: Both are C4H10, but one is a straight chain (butane) and the other is branched (isobutane), so they are constitutional isomers. No C=C or ring is present, so cis–trans is not possible.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Name both. Writing a chain from the other end does not change the molecule.
w: Both are a 4-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2 (2-methylbutane), written left-to-right and right-to-left: the same compound. Different-looking condensed formulas are not automatically isomers.

q: In one molecule of CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are on the same side of the double bond; in another they are on opposite sides. These two molecules are
h: Same formula and same connections; the only difference is the arrangement around a C=C that cannot rotate.
w: Same side = cis-2-butene, opposite sides = trans-2-butene. The atoms are connected identically, so they are cis–trans isomers, not constitutional isomers. Without free rotation around C=C they cannot interconvert, so they are not the same compound.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Isomers must have the same molecular formula. Count the hydrogens.
w: 2-Butene is C4H8 and butane is C4H10. Different formulas, so they are unrelated (not isomers). Same number of carbons is not enough.

q: Which compound can exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups.
w: In ClCH=CHCl each double-bond carbon has H and Cl, so the Cl atoms can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans): ClCH=CHCl. In the others at least one carbon has two identical groups (two H or two Cl).

q: Ethanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is a functional-group isomer of which compound?
h: Find the compound with the same formula, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O, but a different functional group.
w: Dimethyl ether CH3OCH3 is C2H6O, like ethanol, but is an ether instead of an alcohol: CH3OCH3. CH3OCH2CH3 is C3H8O and CH3CHO is C2H4O.

q: Which compound is a constitutional isomer of propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO?
h: Propanal is C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. Aldehydes and ketones with the same number of carbons are often isomers.
w: Acetone (propanone) CH3COCH3 is also C3H6O, with a ketone in place of the aldehyde: CH3COCH3. 1-Propanol is C3H8O (two more H) and propanoic acid has an extra O.

q: Propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, has the same molecular formula as which ester?
h: Write the formula of propanoic acid, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, then count the C atoms in each ester, including the alkyl group on O.
w: Methyl ethanoate CH3COOCH3 is C3H6O2, a functional-group isomer of propanoic acid: CH3COOCH3. Methyl propanoate has 4 carbons because the methyl on O counts too.

q: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O can be an aldehyde or a ketone. Including branched skeletons, how many such carbonyl compounds exist?
h: Draw every four-carbon skeleton and place a C=O: at the end of a chain (aldehyde) or in the middle (ketone).
w: Aldehydes: CH3CH2CH2CHO and (CH3)2CHCHO; ketone: CH3COCH2CH3. Total = 3. C=O on C2 from the other end is the same butanone, not a new compound.

q: Butanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, are best described as
h: Count the atoms in each. Same molecular formula? Then decide whether the atoms are connected the same way.
w: Both are C4H8O, but the C=O is at the end in one and in the middle in the other, so they are constitutional isomers (different functional groups, even). Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or ring with the same connections.

q: A student writes 2-butanol two ways: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. How are these two formulas related?
h: Name each one. Writing a condensed formula from the other end does not make a new molecule.
w: Both are a four-carbon chain with –OH on the second carbon: 2-butanol written from opposite ends. They are the same compound. Isomers would need a different connection, such as 1-butanol.

q: Cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is a saturated ring. Which compound below is its constitutional isomer?
h: Isomers must have exactly the same molecular formula. Count C and H in each choice.
w: A ring and a C=C each remove 2 H from the alkane formula, so an open-chain alkene has the same formula as a cycloalkane. 1-Hexene is C6H12; hexane is C6H14, cyclohexene C6H10 and benzene C6H6.

q: Replacing one H of a C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkane with Br gives C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Br. Counting all carbon skeletons, how many structurally different bromides are possible?
h: Draw the three C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> skeletons, then put Br on each different kind of carbon in each skeleton.
w: Pentane: Br on C1, C2 or C3 (3). 2-Methylbutane: four different carbon positions (4). 2,2-Dimethylpropane: all CH3 are equal (1). Total = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8. Answering 3 counts only the straight chain.

q: Which of these alkene names is invalid, because the molecule cannot have cis and trans forms?
h: Cis–trans isomerism needs each C=C carbon to carry two different groups.
w: In 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, C2 carries two identical CH3 groups, so swapping sides gives the same molecule. cis-2-Methyl-2-butene is therefore not a valid name. In the other three, each C=C carbon has two different groups (e.g. 3-methyl-2-pentene: H/CH3 on C2, CH3/CH2CH3 on C3).

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Write the molecular formula of each. Same formula with different connections means one thing; identical connections means another.
w: Both are C5H12, but I is an unbranched chain (pentane) and II has four carbons bonded to one central carbon (2,2-dimethylpropane). Same formula, different connections: constitutional isomers. They are not the same compound, because no bonds can be rotated to turn one into the other.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Find the longest continuous carbon chain in each drawing, even if it turns a corner at a branch.
w: In II the longest chain runs through the "ethyl" branch: it is six carbons with a CH3 on C3, exactly like I. Both are 3-methylhexane, so they are the same compound drawn two ways. Students who only compare how the drawings look call them constitutional isomers.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Count C, H and O in each. Then look at what the O is bonded to.
w: Both are C3H8O. In I the O carries an H (an alcohol, 1-propanol); in II the O is between two carbons (an ether, ethyl methyl ether). Same formula, different connections: constitutional isomers.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: A ring and a double bond each remove two H atoms from the alkane formula. Compare the molecular formulas.
w: Cyclohexane (I) and 1-hexene (II) are both C6H12, but one has a ring and the other a C=C: constitutional isomers. Students who think a ring compound can only be an isomer of another ring miss this.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Count the hydrogens: every corner of the ring is a CH<sub>2</sub>. What about the open chain?
w: Cyclohexane (I) is C6H12; hexane (II) is C6H14. Different molecular formulas, so they are different compounds, not isomers. Having the same number of carbons is not enough.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Number each chain from the end nearest the OH. Which carbon holds it in each drawing?
w: Both are five-carbon chains with the OH on C2 (2-pentanol); II is simply drawn from the other end. They are the same compound drawn two ways. Flipping a drawing left-to-right never makes an isomer.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Both have a C=O. Write each molecular formula, then ask where the C=O sits.
w: Butanal (I, an aldehyde: C=O at the end) and butanone (II, a ketone: C=O inside the chain) are both C4H8O: constitutional isomers. Students who see two different functional groups sometimes say "not isomers", but only the formula matters.

q: 2-Methylpentane is shown. Which structure is a constitutional isomer of it?
h: An isomer needs the same molecular formula but a different structure. Watch for a drawing of the same molecule turned around.
w: 2-Methylpentane is C6H14. Moving the branch to C3 gives 3-methylpentane, also C6H14: an isomer. The drawing with the branch on the second carbon from the left end is 2-methylpentane again (same compound, not an isomer); 2-methylbutane is C5H12, and the alkene is C6H12.

q: Ethyl acetate, shown, is the solvent in many nail-polish removers. Which compound is a constitutional isomer of it?
h: Write the molecular formula of ethyl acetate first. Then find the choice with exactly the same C, H and O counts.
w: Ethyl acetate is C4H8O2, and so is butanoic acid (esters and carboxylic acids with the same carbons are isomers). Butanal (C4H8O) has one O too few, ethyl propanoate has an extra CH2, and 1-butanol is C4H10O.

q: Cyclopentane, shown, is a constitutional isomer of which compound?
h: A ring removes two H atoms from the alkane formula, just like one double bond does.
w: Cyclopentane is C5H10; 1-pentene is also C5H10, so they are isomers. Cyclopentene (C5H8) has a ring and a C=C; pentane (C5H12) has neither; methylcyclopentane has six carbons.

q: Which structure is cis-2-pentene?
h: In a cis alkene, the two carbon chains attached to the C=C carbons are on the same side of the double bond.
w: In cis-2-pentene the CH3 (C1) and the CH2CH3 (C4–C5) are on the same side of the C2=C3 bond, giving a U-shaped drawing. The zig-zag with the groups on opposite sides is trans-2-pentene; 1-pentene and 2-methyl-2-butene cannot be cis or trans at all.

q: Which structure is trans-4-methyl-2-pentene?
h: Find the C2=C3 double bond. In the trans isomer, the chain carbons on each end point to opposite sides.
w: In trans-4-methyl-2-pentene the CH3 on C2 and the isopropyl group on C3 lie on opposite sides of the C=C. The drawing with them on the same side is the cis isomer. Moving the double bond to C1 or to the branched carbon gives alkenes with no cis/trans form.

q: Which alkene cannot exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Look at each carbon of the C=C. If one of them holds two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule.
w: In 2-methyl-2-butene, one C=C carbon carries two CH3 groups, so there is no "same side" vs. "opposite side" difference. The other three each have two different groups on both C=C carbons, so they can be cis or trans (as drawn, two are trans and one is cis).

q: Which of these alkenes has no cis and trans forms?
h: A double bond at the very end of a chain has a CH<sub>2</sub>= carbon. What are its two groups?
w: In 1-butene, C1 holds two H atoms, so flipping groups across the C=C gives the same molecule. 2-Butene, 2-hexene and 3-methyl-2-pentene each have two different groups on both carbons of the C=C, so they show cis–trans isomerism. A branch alone does not prevent it.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Same formula and same connections? Then look at which side of the C=C each CH<sub>3</sub> is on.
w: Both are 2-butene, C4H8, with identical connections. In I the CH3 groups are on the same side (cis); in II they are on opposite sides (trans). The C=C cannot rotate, so these are cis–trans isomers, not the same compound and not constitutional isomers.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Turn one drawing over in your mind. Are the carbon groups on the same side or opposite sides of the C=C in each?
w: Both drawings have the CH3 and CH2CH3 on opposite sides of C2=C3: both are trans-2-pentene, just flipped. They are the same compound drawn two ways. Calling them cis–trans isomers comes from comparing which way the drawings point instead of the sides of the C=C.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Before looking at wedges, check where the methyl groups are attached. Are they on neighboring ring carbons in both?
w: Both are C8H16, but in I the methyls are on neighboring ring carbons (1,2) and in II they are separated by one CH2 (1,3). Different connections make them constitutional isomers; the matching wedges do not matter.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Find which ring carbons carry the OH groups in each drawing before thinking about wedges and dashes.
w: Both are C5H10O2. In I the OH groups are on neighboring ring carbons (1,2); in II a CH2 separates them (1,3). Different connections means constitutional isomers; stereo terms only apply when the connections match.

q: How many different compounds with the formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> exist, if cis and trans forms are counted separately?
h: Put both Cl on one carbon, or one on each. If one on each, can they be on the same side or opposite sides?
w: 1,1-Dichloroethene (both Cl on the same carbon), cis-1,2-dichloroethene and trans-1,2-dichloroethene: 3. Forgetting that 1,2-dichloroethene has cis and trans forms gives 2; 1,1-dichloroethene has no cis/trans forms because one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups (H, H).
